bibl.title: Predicted growth in plastic waste exceeds efforts to mitigate plastic pollution

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how much plastic enters the world's rivers, lakes and oceans each year, and whether any combination of the mitigation strategies now being adopted can bring that number down by 2030
span.quote: We estimate that ~19 to 23 Mt, or 11%, of plastic waste generated globally in 2016 entered aquatic ecosystems (Fig. 1 and table S4; see the supplementary materials).

span.label: what level of effort in waste reduction, waste management and environmental recovery would be needed to hold emissions below a stated target, given projected growth
span.quote: We assessed the impact of three broad management strategies, plastic waste reduction, waste management, and environmental recovery, at different levels of effort to estimate plastic emissions to 2030 for 173 countries. We estimate that 19 to 23 million metric tons, or 11%, of plastic waste generated globally in 2016 entered aquatic ecosystems. Considering the ambitious commitments currently set by governments, annual emissions may reach up to 53 million metric tons per year by 2030.

span.label: a mechanistic model over 173 countries showing that 19 to 23 Mt entered aquatic ecosystems in 2016, that the world's existing ambitious commitments still leave 20 to 53 Mt/year in 2030, and that no single strategy reaches the target alone
span.quote: We estimate that ~19 to 23 Mt, or 11%, of plastic waste generated globally in 2016 entered aquatic ecosystems (Fig. 1 and table S4; see the supplementary materials).

span.label: prediction
span.quote: We assessed the impact of three broad management strategies, plastic waste reduction, waste management, and environmental recovery, at different levels of effort to estimate plastic emissions to 2030 for 173 countries. We estimate that 19 to 23 million metric tons, or 11%, of plastic waste generated globally in 2016 entered aquatic ecosystems. Considering the ambitious commitments currently set by governments, annual emissions may reach up to 53 million metric tons per year by 2030.

span.label: a flux whose measured size depends entirely on where the boundary of `the environment` is drawn - an order of magnitude between emissions to the ocean and emissions to aquatic ecosystems
span.quote: Our estimate is larger because it includes the amount that accumulates in lakes and rivers in addition to the plastic that escapes to the ocean.

span.label: a distance-based probability function over spatially explicit waste generation and downhill flow accumulation, applied to 173 countries stratified by World Bank income status, with a Monte Carlo simulation propagating parameter uncertainty
span.term: a distance-based probability function over spatially explicit waste generation and downhill flow accumulation, applied to 173 countries stratified by World Bank income status, with a Monte Carlo simulation propagating parameter uncertainty
span.quote: For 173 countries with available data, we calculated annual plastic emissions entering aquatic ecosystems using a distance-based probability function. This function estimates the proportion of inadequately managed waste to reach the nearest aquatic ecosystem based on spatially explicit waste generation and downhill flow accumulation [( 18, 19); see the supplementary materials; figs. S1 and S2]. That is, the closer to an aquatic ecosystem that waste is generated and inadequately managed, the greater the probability it will enter that aquatic ecosystem.

span.label: no environmentally acceptable level of plastic emission has ever been defined, so the paper sets its target to the 2010 ocean figure - chosen because that number galvanized global action. Every statement of the form `the effort required to reach the target` is therefore an effort required to return to a past level, not to a safe one, and the authors say so in the sentence that adopts it
span.term: a target with no threshold behind it
span.quote: Because an environmentally acceptable threshold has yet to be defined, we set the target scenario to 8 million metric tons (Mt), the estimated global emissions in 2010 to the oceans [(16); a subset of aquatic ecosystems considered here] that galvanized global action on plastic pollution by a variety of stakeholders (7).

span.label: river emissions to the ocean run 0.8 to 2.7 Mt/year; emissions to aquatic ecosystems run 19 to 23. The difference is not measurement, it is whether a lake or a river is a destination or a conduit - and two papers using the same data can disagree tenfold without either being wrong
span.term: the boundary is worth an order of magnitude
span.quote: Our estimate is larger because it includes the amount that accumulates in lakes and rivers in addition to the plastic that escapes to the ocean.

span.label: reduction alone needs an 85% cut in waste generation across all income levels; waste management alone needs 99% of plastic waste managed in every country; recovery alone needs 85% of annual emissions pulled back out. Each is stated as a single number, and each is what makes the combined 40/35/25, 99/80/60, 40% package the paper's actual finding
span.quote: If additional actions were to solely focus on reduction, then plastic waste generation would need to be reduced by 85% across all income levels. If additional actions were to solely focus on waste management, then every country would have to make exceptional efforts to properly manage ≥99% of its plastic waste. If ad ditional actions were to solely focus on recovery, then 85% of annual global emissions would have to be recovered from the environment by 2030 (table S3; see the supplementary materials). Although many stakeholders heavily promote only one of these strategies as the“best one,” these results demonstrate that drastic reductions in future plastic emissions cannot be achieved with any one strategy independently (Table 1).

span.label: the G7 charter, the EU strategy, UNEP, Clean Seas and the Our Oceans conferences generally lack specific numerical targets and not all countries have made commitments, so the ambitious scenario had to be built by applying reduction targets by income band. THE MODEL'S INPUT IS AN INTERPRETATION OF POLICY, because policy did not supply a number
span.term: commitments without numbers cannot be modelled
span.quote: Because these commitments generally lack specific numerical targets and not all countries have made commitments

span.label: waste trade is not counted, primary microplastics are not counted, lost fishing gear is not counted, the informal sector is not counted. The authors state the values may be an underestimate - and every named omission is an input, not an output, so the direction of the bias is knowable even where its size is not
span.term: the excluded flows all point the same way
span.quote: We do not include primary microplastics, microplastics produced from the wear of products still in use, or microplastics entering the environment through wastewater, although these are likely comparatively small in mass.

span.label: no environmentally acceptable threshold for plastic emissions has been defined, so the target is a historical figure rather than a safety level
span.quote: Because an environmentally acceptable threshold has yet to be defined, we set the target scenario to 8 million metric tons (Mt), the estimated global emissions in 2010 to the oceans [(16); a subset of aquatic ecosystems considered here] that galvanized global action on plastic pollution by a variety of stakeholders (7).

span.label: the trade of plastic waste is not accounted for, so high-income countries' contributions are misrepresented
span.quote: However, the trade of plastic waste was not accounted for in the current model (see the supplementary materials). Waste shipped predominantly from HI to UMI, LMI, and LI countries for processing may enter into a country with no formal waste management system or one that is less tractable, therefore misrepresenting HI countries’contributions to plastic emissions (22).

span.label: global-scale data on plastic waste generation, collection and disposal are often lacking or unreliable, with inconsistent reporting, differing methodologies and omitted values
span.quote: Global scale data for plastic waste generation, collection, and disposal are often lacking or unreliable because of inconsistencies in reporting among countries, differences in methodologies and units used in reporting, and omitted values (2, 18).

span.label: primary microplastics, wear particles and wastewater microplastic inputs are excluded
span.quote: We do not include primary microplastics, microplastics produced from the wear of products still in use, or microplastics entering the environment through wastewater, although these are likely comparatively small in mass.

span.label: the commitments the ambitious scenario is built from generally lack specific numerical targets, and not all countries have made any
span.quote: Because these commitments generally lack specific numerical targets and not all countries have made commitments

span.quote: However, all commitments to date lack a quantitative model that connects these actions to a measurable reduction in plastic emissions.

span.label: downhill flow accumulation from hydrological modelling, used here as a probability that inadequately managed waste reaches the nearest water body

span.quote: This requires plastic waste generation to be reduced by 40% in HI, 35% in UMI and LMI, and 25% in LI countries compared with the BAU trajectory.
